arXiv:2404.00907v1 [math.AP] 01 Apr 2024

The long-time behavior of solutions of a three-component reaction-diffusion model for the population dynamics of farmers and hunter-gatherers: the different motility case

Dongyuan Xiao    Ryunosuke Mori
Abstract

In this paper, we investigate the spreading properties of solutions of the Aoki-Shida-Shigesada model. This model is a three-component reaction-diffusion system that delineates the geographical expansion of an initially localized population of farmers into a region occupied by hunter-gatherers. By considering the scenario where farmers and hunter-gatherers possess identical motility, Aoki et al. previously concluded, through numerical simulations and some formal linearization arguments, that there are four different types of spreading behaviors depending on the parameter values. In this paper, we concentrate on the general case for which farmers and hunter-gatherers possess different motility. By providing more sophisticated estimates, we not only theoretically justify for the spreading speed of the Aoki-Shida-Shigesada model, but also establish sharp estimates for the long-time behaviors of solutions. These estimates enable us to validate all four types of spreading behaviors observed by Aoki et al..

Key words: Farmer and hunter-gatherer model; long time behavior; spreading speed;  logarithmic correction

1 Introduction

In 1996, Aoki, Shida and Shigesada [2] proposed the following three-component reaction-diffusion system to study the process of Neolithic transition from hunter-gatherers to farmers (actually, in [2], they only considered the with case with same diffusion rate Df=Dc=DhD_{f}=D_{c}=D_{h}, but in the present paper we formulate the problem with different diffusion speeds):

{∂tF=Df​∂x​xF+rf​F​(1−(F+C)/K),∂tC=Dc​∂x​xC+rc​C​(1−(F+C)/K)+e⁡(F+C)​H,in​ℝ.∂tH=Dh​∂x​xH+rh​H​(1−H/L)−e⁡(F+C)​H,\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}F=D_{f}\partial_{xx}F+r_{f}F(1-(F+C)/K),\\ &\partial_{t}C=D_{c}\partial_{xx}C+r_{c}C(1-(F+C)/K)+e(F+C)H,\ \ \ \ \ \ \mbox{in}\ \mathbb{R}.\\ &\partial_{t}H=D_{h}\partial_{xx}H+r_{h}H(1-H/L)-e(F+C)H,\end{aligned}\right.

The population densities of initial farmers, converted farmers and hunter-gatherers are represented by FF, CC and HH, respectively. This model contains nine positive parameters: DfD_{f}, DcD_{c} and DhD_{h} are the diffusion coefficients; rfr_{f}, rcr_{c} and rhr_{h} are the intrinsic growth rates; KK and LL are the carrying capacities of farmers and hunter-gatherers; ee is the conversion rate of hunter-gatherers to farmers. Note that, in [2], DhD_{h} is always assumed to be equal to DcD_{c} and DfD_{f}. However, it is more natural to imagine that hunter-gatherers possess a different motility with farmers.

As shown in [2], by a suitable change of variables, the above system is converted to:

{∂tF=∂x​xF+a​F​(1−F−C),∂tC=dc​∂x​xC+C⁡(1−F−C)+s​H​(F+C),∂tH=dh​∂x​xH+b​H​(1−H−g⁡(F+C)),inℝ,\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}F=\partial_{xx}F+aF(1-F-C),\\ &\partial_{t}C=d_{c}\partial_{xx}C+C(1-F-C)+sH(F+C),\\ &\partial_{t}H=d_{h}\partial_{xx}H+bH(1-H-g(F+C)),\end{aligned}\right.\quad\quad\mbox{in}\ \ \mathbb{R}, (1.1)

where dc=Dc/Dfd_{c}=D_{c}/D_{f}, dh=Dh/Dfd_{h}=D_{h}/D_{f}, a=rf/rca=r_{f}/r_{c}, b=rh/rcb=r_{h}/r_{c}, s=e​L/rcs=eL/r_{c} and g=e​K/rhg=eK/r_{h}. We consider the following initial condition

H(0,x)≡1,C(0,x)≡0,F(0,x)=F0(x)≥0(F0≢0),H(0,x)\equiv 1,\ \ C(0,x)\equiv 0,\ \ F(0,x)=F_{0}(x)\geq 0\ \ \ \ (F_{0}\not\equiv 0), (1.2)

where F0​(x)F_{0}(x) is a compactly supported continuous function. Such initial data indicates a localized population of farmers in a region that was originally occupied by hunter-gatherers.

The ODE system related to the system (1.1) possesses the following four different types of steady states:

(F,C,H)={(0,0,0),(0,0,1),(F^,C^,0),whereF^+C^=1,F^≥0,C^≥0,(0,C∗,H∗),whereC∗=(1+s)/(1+s​g),H∗=(1−g)/(1+s​g).(F,C,H)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &(0,0,0),\ (0,0,1),\\ &(\widehat{F},\widehat{C},0),\ \ \mbox{where}\ \ \widehat{F}+\widehat{C}=1,\ \widehat{F}\geq 0,\ \widehat{C}\geq 0,\\ &(0,C^{*},H^{*}),\ \ \mbox{where}\ \ C^{*}=(1+s)/(1+sg),\ H^{*}=(1-g)/(1+sg).\end{aligned}\right.

The first two steady states always exist and unstable. The third one is a line of neutral equilibria, which always exists and stable if g≥1g\geq 1. The fourth one exists and is stable if and only if g<1g<1. As noted in [17], we call the case g≥1g\geq 1 by high conversion rate case and the case g<1g<1 by low conversion rate case throughout this paper.

1.1 Previous works

In the previous paper [2], Aoki et al. observed four different types of spreading behaviors depending on the parameter values, namely those of aa, ss and gg in (1.1) under the assumption that dc=dh=1d_{c}=d_{h}=1. Furthermore, by mainly on numerical simulations, but also some formal analysis of the minimal speed of the traveling wave, they found the speed of the spreading fronts is determined by max⁡{2​a,2​1+s}\max\{2\sqrt{a},2\sqrt{1+s}\}. In our previous work [17], for the first time, we made mathematically rigorous studies to justify their claims with the same assumption on diffusion speeds. The following figures illustrate the shape of what they call the transient fronts.

In order to make our motivation clearer, we give a brief explanation of the numerical observations by Aoki et al. [2] and our previous theoretical results in [17] before stating our main results.

  • (1)

    Theorem 1.5 in [17] indicates that the behaviors of solutions on the leading edge where hunter-gatherers have little contact with the farmers are almost the same between the high conversion rate case and the low conversion rate case (see Figure 1-4, Leading edge).

  • (2)

    Theorem 1.6 in [17] indicates that the spreading speed of the solution of (1.1) is always determined by max⁡{2​a,2​1+s}\max\{2\sqrt{a},2\sqrt{1+s}\}.

  • (3)

    As showed in Figure 2 and Figure 4, in the case a<1+sa<1+s, a wave of advance of initial farmers FF is not generated (see Theorem 1.9 and 1.10 in [17]). If, in addition that g<1g<1 very small, initial farmers FF disappear entirely, and converted farmers CC and hunter-gatherers HH converge to a positive steady state (see Figure 4). Whereas, if g≥1g\geq 1, behind the wavefront, farmers have almost reached carrying capacity and hunter-gatherers have just disappeared (see Figure 2, Final zone).

  • (4)

    In the case a>1+sa>1+s, an advancing wavefront of initial farmers FF is also generated (see Figure 1 and Figure 3). However, in [17], we can only obtain an advancing wavefront formed by both initial farmers and converted farmers G=F+CG=F+C. If, in addition that g<1g<1, the waveform is a small peak with leading edge and trailing edge that converge to 00 (see Theorem 1.8 in [17]).

In particular, for the case a=1a=1 and dc=1d_{c}=1, by adding the both sides of FF-equation and CC-equation of (1.1), we get

{∂tG=∂x​xG+G⁡(1+s​H−G),∂tH=dh​∂x​xH+b​H​(1−H−g​G),inℝ.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}G=\partial_{xx}G+G(1+sH-G),\\ &\partial_{t}H=d_{h}\partial_{xx}H+bH(1-H-gG),\end{aligned}\right.\quad\quad\mbox{in}\ \ \mathbb{R}. (1.3)

The spreading speed of (1.3) has been studied by Chen et al. in [7]. Without constructing super and sub-solution and applying the comparison argument, they introduced some Harnack type inequalities that can locate the spreading front of some general reaction-diffusion systems.

Remark 1.1

We would like to explain more on the numerical simulation showed in the case where g≥1g\geq 1 and a<1+sa<1+s (see Figure 2). The numerical calculation was done in bounded domain and it would stop at the moment TT when the wavefronts of the solution reached a certain point x0∈[0,l]x_{0}\in[0,l]. Therefore, one may find that initial farmers FF still exist in the final zone. As a matter of fact,, we will prove in the present paper that the population density of initial farmers FF converges to 00 uniformly for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} (see Theorem 1.7). The sharp estimate given in Theorem 1.9 indicates that FF decreases to 00 with polynomial order for |x|≤t12|x|\leq t^{\frac{1}{2}}, but with exponential order for |x|>t12+δ|x|>t^{\frac{1}{2}+\delta}, δ>0\delta>0 very small. This explain the reason why we can observe a bump on profiles of FF and CC.

Remark 1.2

The goal of the present paper is to give rigorous justification to all of the above observations for the case dc≠1d_{c}\neq 1 and dh≠1d_{h}\neq 1. The behaviors of solutions on the leading edge showed on Figure 1-4 can be justified by Theorem 1.4, which also provides an upper estimate on the spreading speed. On the other hand, the lower estimate on the spreading speed will be given in Theorem 1.5. The behaviors of solutions in the final zone showed on Figure 2 and 4 can be justified by Theorem 1.7 by dealing with the case g≥1g\geq 1 and g<1g<1, respectively.

1.2 Main results

In this subsection, we will recall some previous works about the spreading properties of solutions of scalar KPP equation and present our main results which are concerned with the spreading speeds and the asymptotic profiles of solutions. Moreover, we will conclude how do our results justify the four different spreading behavior.

Front propagation for scalar reaction-diffusion equations has been studied extensively and there exist vast literature on this theme. Early in 1937, Fisher [11] and Kolmogorov, Petrovsky and Piskunov [16] introduced a scalar reaction-diffusion equation with monostable nonlinearity as a model equation in population genetics, which studies the propagation of dominant gene in a homogeneous environment. In particular, [16] made an important early analysis of the structure of the set of traveling waves for a special class of monostable reaction-diffusion equation, the so-called KPP equation. Application of reaction-diffusion equations to ecology was pioneered by Skellam [18] in 1951. As regards the propagation of fronts for solutions with compactly supported initial data (that is, the so-called “spreading front”) is concerned, the first rigorous mathematical results in multi-dimensional homogeneous environment were provided by Aronson and Weinberger [3], for the case of monostable nonlinearity and also for bistable nonlinearity.

As regards the propagation of fronts for solutions of the reaction-diffusion system, there exists a rich literature on the cooperate system and the competition system, for which the comparison principle still hold. However, apart from some recent works such as [9], much less is known about the spreading properties for systems for which the comparison principle does not hold.

We first recall the classical spreading result for the monostable scalar equation from Aronson and Weinberger [3]:

Proposition 1.3 (Spreading for the scalar KPP equation ([3]))

Consider the so-called KPP equation

∂tu⁡(t,x)=d​∂x​xu⁡(t,x)+f⁡(u⁡(t,x)),t>0,x∈ℝ,\partial_{t}u(t,x)=d\partial_{xx}u(t,x)+f(u(t,x)),\ t>0,\ x\in\mathbb{R}, (1.4)

wherein f∈C1​(ℝ)f\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}) satisfies

f(0)=f(1)=0,f(u)>0andf′(u)≤f′(0)for allu∈(0,1).f(0)=f(1)=0,\ f(u)>0\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ f^{\prime}(u)\leq f^{\prime}(0)\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ u\in(0,1).

Define c∗​(d,f)=2​d​f′​(0)c^{*}(d,f)=2\sqrt{df^{\prime}(0)}. Then, for any nontrivial compactly supported and continuous initial data u0​(x)u_{0}(x), the solution u≡u⁡(t,x,u0​(x))u\equiv u(t,x;u_{0}(x)) of (1.4):

limt→+∞​sup|x|≤c​t​|1−u⁡(t,x)|=0, 0<c<c∗​(d,f),\underset{t\to+\infty}{\lim}\underset{|x|\leq ct}{\sup}|1-u(t,x)|=0,\ 0<c<c^{*}(d,f),

and

limt→+∞​sup|x|≥c​t​u​(t,x)=0,c>c∗​(d,f).\underset{t\to+\infty}{\lim}\underset{|x|\geq ct}{\sup}u(t,x)=0,\ c>c^{*}(d,f).

Moreover, the so-called spreading speed c∗​(d,f)c^{*}(d,f) coincides with the minimal speed of the traveling wave solution of admitted by (1.4).

Next, we present our main results on the spreading properties of solutions of the system (1.1). Throughout this paper, we define cf:=2​ac_{f}:=2\sqrt{a}, cc:=2​dc​(1+s)c_{c}:=2\sqrt{d_{c}(1+s)}, and c∗:=max⁡{cf,cc}c^{*}:=\max\{c_{f},c_{c}\}. The following Theorem 1.4 and Theorem 1.5 can be regarded as an analogue of the well-known "hair-trigger effect" for scalar monostable equation [3]. Moreover, since H0​(x)≡1H_{0}(x)\equiv 1, one may find that the spreading speed of (1.1) is always determined by the larger value of cfc_{f} and ccc_{c}, which is only determined by the parameters in the FF-equation and CC-equation.

Our first result is concerned with the analysis of the leading edge, which provides an upper estimate on the spreading speed. As we observed from Figure 11-44, for all four cases, the behaviors of solutions are almost same on the leading edge.

Theorem 1.4

Let (F,C,H)(F,C,H) be the solution of (1.1) with the initial data satisfying (1.2). Then for any 2​a<c12\sqrt{a}<c_{1} and c∗<c2c^{*}<c_{2}, it holds:

lim supt→∞supc1​t≤|x|F⁡(t,x)=0,\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{c_{1}t\leq|x|}F(t,x)=0, (1.5)
lim supt→∞supc2​t≤|x|(C⁡(t,x)+|1−H⁡(t,x)|)=0.\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{c_{2}t\leq|x|}\Big(C(t,x)+|1-H(t,x)|\Big)=0. (1.6)

The most difficult part of the analysis is the behaviors of the solutions in the final zone, where hunter-gatherers, initial farmers and converted farmers heavily interact with each other. A large part of this paper is devoted to the analysis in this region. Our second result deals with the propagation of farmers in the final zone, which provides a lower estimate on the spreading speed.

Let (F,C,H)(F,C,H) be the solution of (1.1) with the initial data satisfying (1.2). Then for any c1<c∗c_{1}<c^{*}, it holds:

The values 2​a2\sqrt{a} and 2​dc​(1+s)2\sqrt{d_{c}(1+s)} indicate the spreading speed of initial farmers and converted farmers respectively. More precisely, if we let C≡0C\equiv 0 in (1.1), then the spreading speed of initial farmers directly comes from the single equation

∂tF=∂x​xF+a​F​(1−F−C).\partial_{t}F=\partial_{xx}F+aF(1-F-C).

{∂tC=dc​∂x​xC+C⁡(1−F−C)+s​H​(F+C),∂tH=dh​∂x​xH+b​H​(1−H−g⁡(F+C)),inℝ.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}C=d_{c}\partial_{xx}C+C(1-F-C)+sH(F+C),\\ &\partial_{t}H=d_{h}\partial_{xx}H+bH(1-H-g(F+C)),\end{aligned}\right.\quad\quad\mbox{in}\ \ \mathbb{R}.

The main results in [7] indicates the spreading speed of converted farmers is equal to 2​dc​(1+s)2\sqrt{d_{c}(1+s)}.

At last, we show our main results about the asymptotic profiles of solutions in the final zone. The precise results will be presented in two cases: the case a>dc​(1+s)a>d_{c}(1+s) and the case a<dc​(1+s)a<d_{c}(1+s), respectively. The critical case a=dc​(1+s)a=d_{c}(1+s) will not be discussed in the present paper. Moreover, for the each case, the profiles of solutions are also depending on the value of gg. For the high conversion rate case, we not only show that all of the original hunter-gatherers convert to farmers at last, but also investigate the explicit profiles (the bump phenomena) of the FF-component and CC-component in the final zone. For the low conversion rate case, we find that the FF converges to 00 global uniformly. Then, we can investigate how the CC and HH behave in the finial zone by considering the dynamics of the underlying ODE system:

{Ct=C⁡(1−C)+s​C​H,Ht=b​H​(1−H−g​C).\left\{\begin{aligned} &C_{t}=C(1-C)+sCH,\\ &H_{t}=bH(1-H-gC).\end{aligned}\right. (1.9)

We expect the solution of the PDE system (1.1) to uniformly converge to the equilibrium (C∗,H∗)(C^{*},H^{*}) in the final zone as t→+∞t\to+\infty. We prove the conjecture by the established fact that a strict Lyapunov function exists.

2 Upper estimates on the spreading speeds

In this section, we deal with the spreading properties of solutions of (1.1) on the leading edge and complete the proof of Theorem 1.4. Since there is little interaction between farmers and hunter-gatherers on the leading edge, the analysis of this zone is rather straightforward.

We first deal with the analysis of FF and CC on the leading edge and begin the proof with some simple upper estimates on the spreading speed. From C≥0C\geq 0 for all (t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝ(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{R}, by a well-known super-solution

F¯:=min⁡{A1​e−a​(|x|−2​a​t),1},\bar{F}:=\min\{A_{1}e^{-\sqrt{a}(|x|-2\sqrt{a}t)},1\}, (2.1)

one has

limt→+∞​sup|x|≥c​t​F​(t,x)≤limt→+∞​sup|x|≥c​t​F¯​(t,x)=0for allc>c∗≥2​a,\underset{t\to+\infty}{\lim}\underset{|x|\geq ct}{\sup}F(t,x)\leq\underset{t\to+\infty}{\lim}\underset{|x|\geq ct}{\sup}\bar{F}(t,x)=0\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ c>c^{*}\geq 2\sqrt{a}, (2.2)

provided that A1A_{1} is large enough such that F¯​(0,x)≥F​(0,x)\bar{F}(0,x)\geq F(0,x). This proves (1.5) in Theorem 1.4.

4 Asymptotic profiles for the case dc​(1+s)>ad_{c}(1+s)>a

We have already shown that the propagation of farmers occurs with the speed c∗c^{*}. However, whether the profiles of solutions converges to the steady states (F^,C^,0)(\widehat{F},\widehat{C},0) or (0,C∗,H∗)(0,C^{*},H^{*}) are still unknown. In this section, we mainly deal with the asymptotic profiles of solutions in the final zone for the case dc​(1+s)>ad_{c}(1+s)>a. According to the numerical work of Aoki et al., the profiles of solutions in the final zone are suppose to be different between the cases g≥1g\geq 1 and g<1g<1. In particular, a bump has been observed in the case g>1g>1.

The justification of the numerical results will be split into several parts. The first part contributes to an upper estimate on FF and lower estimate on CC, which holds for all g>0g>0. In particular, we will show that FF uniformly converges to 00 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, which will play an important role in investigating the asymptotic profiles of CC and HH in the final zone.

4.1 The upper estimate on FF and the lower estimate on CC

Throughout this subsection, we let max⁡{cf,2​dc}<c0<cc\max\{c_{f},2\sqrt{d_{c}}\}<c_{0}<c_{c} be fixed. First of all, we will show FF uniformly converges to 00 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} by comparing with the solution of a system as follows:

{ut=ux​x+a​u​(1−u−v),vt=dc​vx​x+v⁡(1−v−u).\left\{\begin{aligned} &u_{t}=u_{xx}+au(1-u-v),\\ &v_{t}=d_{c}v_{xx}+v(1-v-u).\\ \end{aligned}\right. (4.1)

The system (4.1) is the so-called critical Lotka-Volterra competition system, for which the Cauchy problem with two compactly supported initial data (u0​(x),v0​(x))(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x)) has been well studied in [1]. More precisely, since u,vu,v have a same competition strength, Alfaro et al. found that the fast species dominates the habitat at last, but the slow one becomes extinct. In other words, if a>dca>d_{c}, then vv uniformly converges to 00; if a<dca<d_{c}, then vv uniformly converges to 00. Note that, in our case, the initial data is not supposed to be two compactly supported functions. However, an a priori estimate on C⁡(t,x)C(t,x) from Proposition 3.2 roughly implies that CC is the fast species.

Let us recall the competitive comparison principle. Define the operators

N1​[u,v]:=∂tu−∂x​xu−u⁡(1−u−v) and N2​[u,v]:=∂tv−dc​∂x​xv−v⁡(1−v−u)N_{1}[u,v]:=\partial_{t}u-\partial_{xx}u-u(1-u-v)\quad\text{ and }\quad N_{2}[u,v]:=\partial_{t}v-d_{c}\partial_{xx}v-v(1-v-u) (4.2)

on the domain Ω:=(t1,t2)×(x1,x2)\Omega:=(t_{1},t_{2})\times(x_{1},x_{2}) with 0≤t1<t2≤+∞0\leq t_{1}<t_{2}\leq+\infty and −∞≤x1<x2≤+∞-\infty\leq x_{1}<x_{2}\leq+\infty. A super-solution is a pair

(u¯,v¯)∈[C1​((t1,t2),C2​((x1,x2)))∩Cb​(Ω¯)]2(\overline{u},\underline{v})\in\Big[C^{1}\Big((t_{1},t_{2}),C^{2}((x_{1},x_{2}))\Big)\cap C_{b}\left(\overline{\Omega}\right)\Big]^{2}

satisfying

N1​[u¯,v¯]≥0andN2​[u¯,v¯]≤0​ in ​Ω.N_{1}[\overline{u},\underline{v}]\geq 0\quad\text{and}\quad N_{2}[\overline{u},\underline{v}]\leq 0\;\text{ in }\Omega.

Similarly, a sub-solution (u¯,v¯)(\underline{u},\overline{v}) satisfies N1​[u¯,v¯]≤0N_{1}[\underline{u},\overline{v}]\leq 0 and N2​[u¯,v¯]≥0N_{2}[\underline{u},\overline{v}]\geq 0.

Let (u¯,v¯)(\overline{u},\underline{v}) and (u¯,v¯)(\underline{u},\overline{v}) be a super-solution and sub-solution satisfying (4.25), respectively. If

and, for i=1,2i=1,2,

If x1=−∞x_{1}=-\infty or x2=+∞x_{2}=+\infty, the corresponding boundary conditions can be omitted.

4.2 The bump phenomena in the high conversion case

In this subsection, we will provide a lower estimate on FF and an upper estimate on CC for the case g>1g>1, which explain the reason why bumps on the profiles of FF and CC are observed by the numerical simulation. A short discussion on the critical case g=1g=1 will be given in Remark 4.7.

The estimate (4.18) implies that HH decreases to 00 uniformly in the final zone. However, to get sharp estimates on FF and CC, we need first show that HH decreases to 00 with an exponential decay rate

4.3 Asymptotic profiles for the low conversion rate case

In this subsection, we deal with the proof of statement (2) in Proposition 1.7. The key point of studying the asymptotic profiles in the low conversion rate case is to provide a uniform lower estimate of HH in the final zone. In our previous study [17], for the general case, we thought it is hard to give the necessary and sufficient condition under which HH is uniform positive from below. In this subsection, we first show that HH is uniformly positive from below for all (t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝ(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{R} if and only if g<1g<1. Then, we show that CC and HH would converge to (C∗,H∗)(C^{*},H^{*}) as t→+∞t\to+\infty in the final zone.

|xn|≤c​tnand|C⁡(tn,xn)−C∗|+|H⁡(tn,xn)−H∗|≥δ.|x_{n}|\leq ct_{n}\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ |C(t_{n},x_{n})-C^{*}|+|H(t_{n},x_{n})-H^{*}|\geq\delta. (4.45)

Consider the sequence of functions (Fn,Cn,Hn)​(t,x)=(F,C,H)​(t+tn,x+xn)(F_{n},C_{n},H_{n})(t,x)=(F,C,H)(t+t_{n},x+x_{n}). Now, let us fix c′>0c^{\prime}>0 such that c<c′<c∗c<c^{\prime}<c^{*}. Therefore, there exist N>0N>0 large enough and ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough such that, for t+tn≥At+t_{n}\geq A and |x|≤c′​t+(c′−c)​tn|x|\leq c^{\prime}t+(c^{\prime}-c)t_{n}, one has Fn​(t,x)≤1nF_{n}(t,x)\leq\frac{1}{n} from Proposition 4.4. Moreover, there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that

ε≤Cn​(t,x)≤1+s−εandε≤Hn​(t,x)≤1−ε.\varepsilon\leq C_{n}(t,x)\leq 1+s-\varepsilon\quad\text{and}\quad\varepsilon\leq H_{n}(t,x)\leq 1-\varepsilon.

Then, by parabolic estimates, possibly along a subsequence, one may assume that

(Fn,Cn,Hn)​(t,x)→(F∞,C∞,H∞)​(t,x)locally uniformly for(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ,(F_{n},C_{n},H_{n})(t,x)\to(F_{\infty},C_{\infty},H_{\infty})(t,x)\ \ \mbox{locally uniformly for}\ \ (t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R},

where (F∞,C∞,H∞)(F_{\infty},C_{\infty},H_{\infty}) is a bounded entire solution and satisfies

sup(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ​F∞​(t,x)=0,\underset{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}}{\sup}F_{\infty}(t,x)=0,
inf(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ​C∞​(t,x)>0andinf(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ​H∞​(t,x)>0,\underset{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}}{\inf}C_{\infty}(t,x)>0\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ \underset{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}}{\inf}H_{\infty}(t,x)>0, (4.46)

Moreover, by (4.45) it holds

|C∞​(0,0)−C∗|+|H∞​(0,0)−H∗|>0.|C_{\infty}(0,0)-C^{*}|+|H_{\infty}(0,0)-H^{*}|>0. (4.47)

However, by applying the Lyapunov function Ψ⁡(C,H)\Psi(C,H) which satisfying (4.42), (4.47) contradicts to the convergence result of Theorem 1.1 in [13]. Therefore, the proof of (2) of Theorem 1.7 is complete. □\square
